title: Rapunzel
paragraphs: Once there was a man and a woman who had wished for a child for a long time, without success. At last the woman began to hope that God was about to grant her wish. At the back of their house they had a little window that looked out on a splendid garden, full of the loveliest flowers and herbs. A high wall surrounded it, and no one dared to enter, because it belonged to an enchantress who had great power and was feared by everyone. One day the woman was standing at this window, looking down into the garden, when she noticed a bed planted with the most beautiful rampion (rapunzel). It looked so fresh and green that she longed for some. She wanted it so much that she pined away and grew pale and miserable. Her husband became alarmed and asked, “What is wrong, dear wife?” “Oh,” she answered, “if I can’t eat some of that rampion from the garden behind our house, I will die.” The man loved her, and he thought, “Rather than let my wife die, I will fetch her some of that rampion, whatever it costs.” At twilight he climbed over the wall into the enchantress’s garden, hurriedly snatched a handful of rampion, and took it to his wife. She made a salad of it at once and ate it greedily. It tasted so good to her, so very good, that the next day she wanted it three times as much as before. If he was ever to have any peace, her husband would have to go down into the garden once more. So in the gloom of evening he lowered himself down again. But when he had climbed down the wall he was terrified, for there stood the enchantress right in front of him. “How dare you,” she said, with an angry look, “climb into my garden and steal my rampion like a thief? You will pay for this!” “Oh,” he answered, “let mercy win out over justice. I only did it because I had to. My wife saw your rampion from the window and wanted it so badly that she would have died if she hadn’t had some to eat.” Then the enchantress let her anger cool and said to him, “If it is as you say, I will let you take as much rampion as you like. But I have one condition: you must give me the child your wife will bring into the world. It will be well treated, and I will look after it like a mother.” In his terror the man agreed to everything. When the woman gave birth, the enchantress appeared at once, named the child Rapunzel, and took her away.

Rapunzel grew up to be the most beautiful child under the sun. When she was twelve years old, the enchantress shut her up in a tower in a forest. It had no stairs and no door, only a little window right at the top. When the enchantress wanted to go in, she stood beneath the window and called:

“Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me.”

Rapunzel had magnificent long hair, as fine as spun gold. When she heard the enchantress’s voice, she undid her braids, wound them around one of the window hooks, and let them fall twenty ells to the ground, and the enchantress climbed up by them.

A year or two later, the king’s son happened to ride through the forest and past the tower. He heard singing so lovely that he stopped to listen. It was Rapunzel, who passed the time in her loneliness by letting her sweet voice ring out. The king’s son wanted to climb up to her and looked for a door into the tower, but there was none. He rode home, but the singing had touched his heart so deeply that he went out into the forest every day to listen to it. One day, as he stood behind a tree, he saw an enchantress arrive, and he heard her call out:

“Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me.”

Then Rapunzel let down her braids, and the enchantress climbed up to her. “If that is the ladder people climb up by, then I will try my luck too,” he said. The next day, as it began to get dark, he went to the tower and called:

“Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me.”
At once the hair fell down, and the king’s son climbed up.

At first Rapunzel was terribly frightened when a man came in, for her eyes had never seen one before. But the king’s son talked to her like a friend. He told her that his heart had been so stirred that he could find no rest and had been forced to see her. Then Rapunzel lost her fear. When he asked whether she would take him as her husband, and she saw that he was young and handsome, she thought, “He will love me more than old Dame Gothel does.” So she said yes and put her hand in his. She said, “I would gladly go away with you, but I don’t know how to get down. Every time you come, bring a skein of silk, and I will weave a ladder from it. When it is finished, I will climb down, and you can take me away on your horse.” They agreed that until then he would come to her every evening, since the old woman came during the day. The enchantress noticed nothing, until one day Rapunzel said to her, “Tell me, Dame Gothel, how is it that you are so much heavier to pull up than the young king’s son? He is up here in a moment.” “Oh, you wicked child!” cried the enchantress. “What do I hear you say? I thought I had cut you off from the whole world, and still you have deceived me!” In her rage she seized Rapunzel’s beautiful hair, wrapped it twice around her left hand, took a pair of scissors in her right, and snip, snap, the hair was cut off and the lovely braids lay on the ground. And she was so merciless that she took poor Rapunzel to a wilderness, where she had to live in great sorrow and misery.
On the same day that she cast Rapunzel out, the enchantress fastened the braids she had cut off to the window hook. When the king’s son came and called:

“Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me.”

she let the hair down. The king’s son climbed up, but instead of finding his dear Rapunzel, he found the enchantress, who stared at him with wicked, venomous eyes. “Aha!” she cried mockingly. “You came to fetch your darling, but the beautiful bird no longer sits singing in her nest. The cat has got her, and it will scratch out your eyes as well. Rapunzel is lost to you. You will never see her again.” The king’s son was beside himself with grief, and in his despair he leapt from the tower. He escaped with his life, but the thorns he fell into pierced his eyes. Then he wandered blind through the forest, eating nothing but roots and berries, and did nothing but lament and weep over the loss of his dearest wife. He roamed in misery like this for some years, and at last he came to the wilderness where Rapunzel lived in wretchedness with the twins she had given birth to, a boy and a girl. He heard a voice, and it seemed so familiar that he walked toward it. When he came close, Rapunzel recognized him, threw her arms around his neck and wept. Two of her tears fell on his eyes, and they grew clear again, and he could see as well as before. He took her to his kingdom, where he was welcomed with joy, and they lived happily and contentedly for a long time after.
